podcast.body: Recorded in a New York studio on August 10, 1920, this song addressed the mistreatment of black people, with a hidden meaning relating to racial injustice rather than just domestic violence. It achieved immediate success, selling 75,000 copies in its first month and over two million copies overall, and was one of the first songs to establish the blues as a popular recorded art form, laying foundations for future blues, R&B, and ultimately rock music. "It was also one of the first songs to establish the blues as a popular art form, at least as in a recorded sense."

podcast.body: Recorded in a New York studio on August 10, 1920, this song by Manny Smith openly addressed the mistreatment of black people. While it appeared to be about domestic violence, substituting "my man" for "the white man or white people" revealed its intended, hidden meaning, making it a powerful social commentary. The song immediately became a sensation, selling 75,000 copies in its first month and over two million copies overall, and was pivotal in establishing the blues as a popular recorded art form, laying foundational elements for future blues, R&B, and rock music. "It sounds like she was singing about domestic violence, but if you substitute my man for the white man or white people, the song takes on its intended hidden meaning."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
